malrules.name: Alignment-Error-In-Multi-Digit
malrules.description: A systematic procedural bug where students correctly compute partial products but fail to align them properly according to place value. When multiplying by the tens digit, students do not shift the partial product one place to the left, treating the tens digit as if it were in the ones place. For example, in 23 × 14, they compute 23×4=92 and 23×1=23, then add 92+23=115 instead of 92+230=322. This error was documented in Brown & Burton's (1978) BUGGY diagnostic system as a common procedural bug in multi-digit arithmetic algorithms.

malrules.name: Divide-Larger-By-Smaller-Always
malrules.description: A persistent misconception where students believe division must always involve a larger dividend divided by a smaller divisor. When presented with problems where the dividend is smaller than the divisor (e.g., 4 ÷ 6), students either reverse the operands or claim the problem is impossible. Fischbein et al. (1985) identified this as stemming from 'primitive intuitive models' where division is associated with sharing larger quantities among smaller groups.

malrules.name: Division-Makes-Smaller
malrules.description: A widespread misconception where students believe division always produces a result smaller than the dividend. Fischbein et al. (1985) identified this as a 'primitive intuitive model' stemming from early division experiences with whole numbers. When dividing by decimals or fractions less than 1 (which mathematically produces a larger result), students reject the correct answer as impossible and switch to multiplication. For example, students find 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 counterintuitive and switch to 4 × 0.5 = 2 instead.

malrules.name: Forget-To-Add-Carried-Number
malrules.description: A systematic procedural bug where students correctly multiply each digit but forget to add the carried (regrouped) value to the next place value. This was identified in Brown & Burton's (1978) BUGGY diagnostic system as one of the most common procedural bugs in arithmetic algorithms. For example, in 23 × 4, the student computes 3×4=12 (write 2, carry 1), then 2×4=8, but forgets to add the carried 1, yielding 82 instead of 92.

malrules.name: Multiplication-Makes-Bigger
malrules.description: A widespread misconception where students believe multiplication always produces a result larger than both factors. Fischbein et al. (1985) identified this as stemming from the 'primitive intuitive model' of multiplication as repeated addition, where results are always larger with whole numbers. When multiplying by decimals or fractions less than 1 (e.g., 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1), students reject the correct answer as impossible because the product is smaller than both factors. They may substitute addition or refuse to accept the mathematically correct result.
